summary: This Best Current Practice gives guidance on whether a security system needs automated key management or whether manual keying is enough. The presumption is that automated management is needed when symmetric cryptography is used, and it explains the exceptions.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4107 guides designers deciding how a security protocol should obtain its keys. It generally favors automatic key management and explains the situations where manually configured keys may still be reasonable.

subtitle: When protocol designers should use automated key management and when manual keys may be justified.

tldr.problem: Protocol designers must decide whether security keys can be configured by hand or need an automated exchange.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC generally recommends automated key management, lists conditions where it is required, and describes limited cases where manual keying may be reasonable.
tldr.outcome: Proposals for manual key management carry a high burden of justification. Manually shared secrets should be at least 128 bits and unpredictable.

facts.label: General recommendation
facts.value: Automated key management SHOULD be used

facts.label: Unpredictability target
facts.value: No better than 50% chance after searching half the key space

today: RFC 4107 is a Best Current Practice published in June 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Key Management Decision
sections.content:
Key management establishes the cryptographic material used to protect a protocol. RFC 4107 gives guidance to IETF working groups and protocol authors deciding whether a system needs automated key management or can rely on manual keying.

The general recommendation is to use automated key management. Manual keying can be acceptable in some circumstances, but its proponents must provide a strong justification in the security considerations of the proposal.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC helps protocol designers choose how a system obtains its security keys. Its default advice is to automate the process unless there is a strong reason not to.

sections.title: What Automation Provides
sections.content:
Automated key management derives short-term session keys, sometimes using long-term keys to authenticate the participants. It can confirm that a peer is present, protect against replay, associate protocol state with a session key, create fresh keys, and negotiate cryptographic algorithms.

Manual key management distributes values by hand and cannot provide these features, or makes them extremely difficult. Automation can also replace keys before an algorithm's usage limits are reached. The RFC gives IKE and Kerberos as examples of automated key management systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Automatic key management can check that a peer is present and create fresh session keys. Manually distributing keys does not provide those protections by itself.

sections.title: When Automation Is Required
sections.content:
Automated key management MUST be used when a party would need to manage a large number of pairwise static keys; when a stream cipher is used; or when an initialization vector might be reused. It is also required when large traffic volumes may force frequent session-key changes, when more than two parties share long-term session keys, or when personnel or devices change frequently.

In general, the RFC says automated key management SHOULD establish session keys. It also warns working groups against designing their own key management schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: Automation is required when manual keys would be difficult to manage or reuse could weaken encryption. It is also required when keys need frequent changes or many people share them.

sections.title: When Manual Keying May Be Reasonable
sections.content:
Manual key management may be reasonable when bandwidth is very limited or round-trip times are very high, when the protected information has low value, when traffic volume over the key's lifetime is very small, or when each deployment is very limited in scale.

The RFC warns that these claims should be treated skeptically. A system using manual keys MUST provide a way to identify the key currently in use. Its design SHOULD also explain how to replace a key, including one that may have been compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: Manual keys may suit a very small system, a low-value secret, or a connection where automated exchanges are costly. The system still needs a clear way to identify and replace keys.

sections.title: Secret Length and Unpredictability
sections.content:
When manual key management uses a long-term shared secret, the secret SHOULD be at least 128 bits. It MUST be an unpredictable random value. The RFC describes the goal as giving an attacker no better than a 50% chance of finding the value after searching half the key space.

The RFC points to BCP 86 for public-key size guidance and BCP 106 for random-number generation guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: A manually shared secret should be at least 128 bits and hard to guess. A value chosen predictably does not meet the RFC's randomness requirement.
